sections.title: Vocabulary: the words themselves
sections.intro: These questions set the words narration uses across the blend: which Eastern, Western and game words reach the page, how they look there, and how the checker holds them. Speech register, names, sound words and set phrases are asked in their own sections.

questions.title: Cultivation words in narration
questions.question: When narration needs a word for qi, the Way or the energy centre, which word does it use?
questions.context: R13-6-WOTR_FIRST puts WOTR's own nouns (Essence, Aether, the Soul Crystal, reserve) 'in preference to anything borrowed'; R48-22 and R53-25 let real names stand where a culture is built on them. Qi is Chinese for vital energy (Korean gi, Japanese ki); the dao is the Way; the dantian (Korean danjeon) is an energy centre below the navel.

options.label: WOTR nouns only
options.consequence: Essence, reserve, the Crystal and the draw everywhere; qi, dao and dantian never reach the page. Eastern cultures sound Eastern through names and customs, and the system keeps one vocabulary.
options.sample: The draw came up through the floor plate and stalled under the boy's ribs. The master laid two fingers there and pressed until it hurt. Essence that had pooled high went down to the Crystal in one cold slide, and his knees shook with it. His reserve had run thin since the night before. Iron at the back of his mouth. "Again," the master said, and went back to the brazier.

options.label: Real loanwords by culture
options.consequence: A Korean hall's scenes say gi and danjeon, a Moto dojo says ki, a Chinese lineage hall says qi, in narration as in speech. WOTR nouns keep the Guild layer. Every word must be correct (R50-01).
options.sample: The gi came up through the floor plate and stalled under the boy's ribs. The master laid two fingers there and pressed until it hurt. What had pooled high went down to the danjeon in one cold slide, and his knees shook with it. His gi had run thin since the night before. Iron at the back of his mouth. "Again," the master said, and went back to the brazier.

options.label: Plain English renderings
options.consequence: Narration translates: breath, the Way, the cinnabar field (the literal sense of dantian). Nothing foreign and no WOTR term for the idea; new readers follow at once, and some system precision goes.
options.sample: The breath came up through the floor plate and stalled under the boy's ribs. The master laid two fingers there and pressed until it hurt. What had pooled high went down to the cinnabar field below his navel in one cold slide, and his knees shook with it. His store of breath had run thin since the night before. Iron at the back of his mouth. "Again," the master said, and went back to the brazier.

options.label: The POV's own word
options.consequence: Narration uses whatever the viewpoint calls it, as R51-18 already does for craft terms: a Hon-guk boy thinks gi and danjeon, an Accord examiner thinks Essence and Crystal. Amends R13-6-WOTR_FIRST for Eastern-stratum POVs.
options.sample: The draw came up through the floor plate and stalled under the boy's ribs. The master laid two fingers there and pressed until it hurt. The gi went down to the danjeon in one cold slide, and his knees shook with it. A Guild clerk would have entered it as Essence settling to the Crystal; his grandmother called it gi coming home. Iron at the back of his mouth. "Again," the master said.

questions.rec_reason: Eastern scenes get Eastern words while the system keeps one vocabulary, and the word a viewpoint reaches for becomes characterisation, which is the blend working at the level of a single noun.

questions.title: Titles and honorifics in narration
questions.question: When narration refers to a teacher or a lord in an Eastern house, does it use the house's own title?
questions.context: R51-21 puts Japanese honorifics in Moto speech; speech belongs to the dialogue section, so this asks only about narration. The archive translates ('Teacher', 'Master Kwon') and uses no suffixes. The forms: Japanese -sama (lord), -dono (formal), sensei (teacher); Korean -nim (respect), seonsaengnim (teacher); Chinese shifu (master).

options.label: English titles
options.consequence: Narration says Master Baek, the lord, Teacher; suffixes stay in mouths. Clear to any reader, and the Eastern houses lose some colour in the lines between speech.
options.sample: He knelt outside the door with the tray going cold across his knees. Through the paper Master Baek coughed twice, wet, and turned a page. Nobody went into that room unasked. A skin had formed on the barley tea. When Master Baek said his name at last, he slid the door a little way and waited again, eyes on the sill.

options.label: The house's own title
options.consequence: Narration calls the person what the POV calls them in his head: Baek-seonsaengnim, Tono, Shifu, romanised and never italic (R50-31, R50-32). Strong flavour; every form must be correct and unstacked (R23-10).
options.sample: He knelt outside the door with the tray going cold across his knees. Through the paper Baek-seonsaengnim coughed twice, wet, and turned a page. Nobody went into that room unasked. A skin had formed on the barley tea. When Seonsaengnim said his name at last, he slid the door a little way and waited again, eyes on the sill.

options.label: Bare name in narration
options.consequence: The Western close-third habit: narration says Baek, and titles and suffixes live only in mouths. Lean and neutral; the gap between how people address him and how the page names him shows.
options.sample: He knelt outside the door with the tray going cold across his knees. Through the paper Baek coughed twice, wet, and turned a page. Nobody went into that room unasked. A skin had formed on the barley tea. When Baek said his name at last, he slid the door a little way and waited again, eyes on the sill.

questions.rec_reason: Address carries rank in these cultures, so keeping it in an Eastern POV's narration is the cheapest strong Eastern signal on the page, and it costs Western readers almost nothing after the first use.

questions.title: Foreign and coined words on the page
questions.question: How does a native or coined word sit in the sentence the first time a reader meets it?
questions.context: Today foreign words appear 'plain, no italics' (R49-49, R50-32), and new terms get meaning 'from context and use only' (R51-15), with zero glosses a scene (R4-13). A gloss is a phrase that explains a word in passing. Translated web fiction often italicises or glosses; Western literary fantasy trusts context.

options.label: Plain, context only
options.consequence: Current law. No italics and no explaining phrase; the scene carries the meaning. Immersive and quick, and now and then a reader guesses wrong for a page.
options.sample: Three nights nobody had sat with him. The keeper had put him in the far niche and gone home to his own fire. Brida took the stool by the door and folded her hands into her sleeves. One more empty night and he would have been kiilut, and every woman in the yard would have known whose house had left him there. She stayed until the lamp guttered.

options.label: Glossed once, then bare
options.consequence: A short explaining phrase at the first use in each book, bare after. Lifts R51-15 and R4-13 for foreign words only. Web-fiction readers never stall; literary readers notice the hand.
options.sample: Three nights nobody had sat with him. The keeper had put him in the far niche and gone home to his own fire. Brida took the stool by the door and folded her hands into her sleeves. One more empty night and he would have been kiilut, a corpse nobody sat with, and every woman in the yard would have known whose house had left him there. She stayed until the lamp guttered.

options.label: Italic at first use
options.consequence: Italic at the first appearance marks the word as foreign, roman after, no gloss. Lifts R49-49 and R50-32; italics then carry thought, emphasis and new words, three signals on one mark.
options.sample: Three nights nobody had sat with him. The keeper had put him in the far niche and gone home to his own fire. Brida took the stool by the door and folded her hands into her sleeves. One more empty night and he would have been *kiilut*, and every woman in the yard would have known whose house had left him there. She stayed until the lamp guttered.

options.label: Context plus a glossary
options.consequence: Prose as in A, plus a glossary at the back of each book and a terms page on the wiki. The page stays clean, and LitRPG readers get the reference they expect.
options.sample: Three nights nobody had sat with him. Brida took the stool by the door and folded her hands into her sleeves. One more empty night and he would have been kiilut, and every woman in the yard would have known whose house had left him there. [Back-of-book glossary: kiilut (Kharven), one of the dead left without the Waiting; the worst thing one Kharven can call another.]

questions.rec_reason: It keeps the immersive page the law already has and adds the lookup that LitRPG and translated-fiction readers rely on, without a gloss in any sentence.

questions.title: Learned tongues beside Latin
questions.question: Does Latin stay the one learned tongue in narration, or does each Eastern stratum get its own?
questions.context: Accord Latin 'may appear anywhere by ear' (R51-19), and new Latin must be real (R50-12). Eastern scholars had their own learned tongue: hanmun (Classical Chinese as written in Korea) and kanbun (Classical Chinese read in Japanese order). Mahuo is a Korean-stratum house.

options.label: Latin only
options.consequence: Accord Latin stays the one learned register on the page; Eastern learning shows in plain English. Consistent with R51-19 as written, and Eastern scholars sound less learned than Accord clerks.
options.sample: The Accord examiner wrote In registro relatum under the reading and sanded it. The Mahuo examiner took the pen after him, wrote four characters in his own hand, and read them out for the room in plain words: knowing and doing are one. The candidate kept his eyes on the table. Ink, sand, and the stove ticking as it cooled.

options.label: A learned tongue per stratum
options.consequence: Hanmun tags for Korean-stratum scholars, kanbun readings in Moto records, Latin for the Accord, each real and romanised (R50-01, R50-31). Every learned culture gets weight; every tag needs checking.
options.sample: The Accord examiner wrote In registro relatum under the reading and sanded it. The Mahuo examiner took the pen after him, wrote four characters in his own hand, and read them out the old way for the room: jihaeng habil. The candidate kept his eyes on the table. Ink, sand, and the stove ticking as it cooled.

options.label: Narration translates them all
options.consequence: Learned tags stay in mouths and documents; narration renders them in English, Latin included. Lifts R51-19 for narration. Even-handed and plain; the Accord loses its Latin colour.
options.sample: The Accord examiner wrote the old entry formula under the reading and sanded it: entered in the register. The Mahuo examiner took the pen after him and wrote four characters in his own hand. Knowing and doing are one. The candidate kept his eyes on the table. Ink, sand, and the stove ticking as it cooled.

questions.rec_reason: The blend needs Eastern scholarship to carry the same authority on the page that Accord Latin already has, and a real classical tag does that in a few syllables.

questions.title: How antique the narration runs
questions.question: How far does narration lean toward period and archaic English, and does that change by culture?
questions.context: R51-01: narration is 'plain, undated English by default', and Eresse and the Moto court 'may take a more antique narration'; R48-13 keeps narration timeless. LitRPG narration is plain and current; Victorian fiction leans period (whilst, upon, a deal of); Tolkien rises to the archaic (inverted word order, old words) at high moments.

options.label: Plain, two exceptions
options.consequence: Current law: plain undated English everywhere but Eresse and the Moto court. Readable and timeless; the period feel comes from objects and prices more than from words.
options.sample: The rider came in at dusk with frost in his beard and his horse blowing white. Smoke stood over every stack in the outer town. He gave his name at the gate, took the skin when it was offered, and drank without wiping the neck. The guard counted his arrows while he drank. Nineteen. He had left with forty.

options.label: Light period wash
options.consequence: Victorian-literary words wherever they fit (whilst, upon, a deal of, presently), heavier at the Moto court and Eresse. Every scene sounds of the Draw Age; overdone, it reads as costume.
options.sample: The rider came in at dusk with frost upon his beard and his horse blowing white. Smoke stood over every stack in the outer town. He gave his name at the gate, took the skin when it was offered him, and drank a deal of it without wiping the neck. Whilst he drank, the guard counted his arrows. Nineteen. He had left with forty.

options.label: A dial per culture
options.consequence: Each Standing Inventory sets plain, period or archaic, and narration follows the POV's culture. The sample is a Moto-court steward watching from the wall under an archaic dial; a Kharven POV stays plain.
options.sample: At dusk came the rider, frost in his beard and his horse blowing white, and over every stack of the outer town stood the smoke. At the gate he gave his name. The skin was offered him, and he drank of it with the neck unwiped. Nineteen arrows in his quiver. Forty had he carried north.

options.label: Plain modern literary
options.consequence: Contemporary literary English everywhere, contractions in narration, plain idiom short of slang; antique words only in mouths and documents. Closest to LitRPG; lifts R51-01's two exceptions.
options.sample: The rider came in at dusk, frost in his beard, his horse blowing white. Smoke hung over every stack in the outer town. He gave his name at the gate and took the skin when they offered it. Didn't wipe the neck. The guard counted his arrows while he drank. Nineteen. He'd gone out with forty.

questions.rec_reason: A dial lets the Moto court sound archaic, the Accord Victorian and the Kharven plain, so the register itself tells East, West and North apart.

questions.title: Fight vocabulary by school
questions.question: Which martial vocabulary names the moves in narration when the fighters are not European-trained?
questions.context: R48-33 traces every exchange by 'its fencing name', and R13-6-HEMA_VOCAB builds on HEMA (Historical European Martial Arts: Vor, Indes, the bind, vom Tag). A Moto or Shirogane blade has Japanese terms: jōdan (high stance), ma-ai (fighting distance), kiri-oroshi (downward cut), tsuba (handguard). verify_scene --combat WARNs on zero HEMA words.

options.label: HEMA for every fight
options.consequence: Current law. Moto, hall and Kharven fights all read in German and Italian fencing words. One exact grammar and a working checker; Eastern schools sound European.
options.sample: The Shirogane man lifted his blade into vom Tag and held it there, still as a post. The measure closed by half a foot. The Accord fencer waited in Pflug, point at the other man's throat. When the high cut started he went Indes, into it, crossing on the forte, and the bind carried the Shirogane blade off its line. His point found the forearm above the guard.

options.label: Each school's own terms
options.consequence: Moto schools in kenjutsu (Japanese swordsmanship) terms, Korean and Chinese halls in theirs, HEMA for Western blades, whoever holds the POV. True to each art; the checker needs Eastern lists.
options.sample: The Shirogane man lifted his blade into jōdan and held it there, still as a post. The ma-ai closed by half a foot. The Accord fencer waited in Pflug, point at the other man's throat. When the kiri-oroshi started he went Indes, into it, crossing on the forte, and the bind carried the Shirogane blade off its line. His point found the forearm above the tsuba.

options.label: The POV's trained vocabulary
options.consequence: Narration names moves in the terms the viewpoint trained in, as R51-18 does for crafts: an Accord fencer reads a Moto stance in HEMA words, a Moto POV reads him in Japanese. Misreadings become characterisation.
options.sample: The Shirogane man lifted his blade into a roof guard, higher and straighter than any Accord manual drew it, and held it there, still as a post. The measure closed by half a foot. The fencer waited in Pflug. When the high cut started he went Indes, crossing on the forte, and the bind carried the foreign blade off its line. His point found the forearm above that small round guard.

options.label: Plain English moves
options.consequence: Narration describes the motion in plain words; fencing names go to mouths, documents and author notes. Readable by anyone; R48-33's trace by fencing name and the --combat check need rewriting.
options.sample: The Shirogane man lifted his blade above his head in both hands and held it there, still as a post. The gap between them closed by half a foot. The Accord fencer waited with his hilt low by his hip, point at the other man's throat. When the downward cut started he stepped into it, crossing blade on blade near his own hilt, and pushed the other sword off its line. His point found the forearm above the guard.

questions.rec_reason: Each art keeps its own words through its own fighters' eyes, and a POV misnaming a foreign school is the read-the-opponent game WOTR already runs on.

questions.title: Units of measure
questions.question: Which units does narration use for distance, weight and time?
questions.context: R49-52: narration 'measures in the POV's own units', with exact figures from 'a trained eye, an instrument, or the notes'; seconds and minutes are free (R51-07); travel runs in miles (R53-08). In-world units already exist: a fire's length, heats, stations. SI is the metric system (metres, kilograms, joules).

options.label: The POV's own units
options.consequence: Current law. A hunter counts in bowshots and a pot's boil, a Measurewright in yards, pounds and joules. Units characterise, and the exact LitRPG-style figure stays with trained eyes.
options.sample: The standpipe stood two bowshots past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked it in the time a pot needed to boil and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, cast iron the size of a man's head, a thing two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a long breath to move.

options.label: Imperial plus WOTR units
options.consequence: Miles, yards, pounds, stone and hours for everyone, and EU and AU/s (WOTR's own units of reserve and rate) for any practitioner. Victorian and familiar; local units fade to flavour.
options.sample: The standpipe stood four hundred yards past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked it in six minutes and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, eight stone of cast iron that two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a full second to move.

options.label: Metric and SI
options.consequence: Metres, kilograms and joules in all narration, the science and LitRPG default and easy to compare across books. Least period-sounding; the Victorian look must carry the period alone.
options.sample: The standpipe stood three hundred and sixty metres past the last stack, its housing furred with frost. The Measurewright walked it in six minutes and set her case on the step. She hung the test weight from the hoist, fifty kilograms of cast iron that two riders had grunted to lift. The needle took a full second to move.

questions.rec_reason: It keeps units as characterisation, gives the trained eye the crisp figures LitRPG readers want, and leaves the common folk their own measures.

questions.title: Numbers: words or digits
questions.question: In narration, are numbers spelled out or written as digits?
questions.context: No rule sets it. The archive spells numbers out in prose and keeps figures such as '3,332 EU' in the author notes. LitRPG prints digits; book style (the Chicago Manual, a standard style guide) spells out small and round numbers. Numbers on screens belong to the LitRPG section; this asks only about prose.

options.label: Words always
options.consequence: Every number in narration spelled out, however large; digits only in documents, instruments and notes. Literary and period; a big exact figure runs long on the page.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to four hundred and twelve rounds, split. Thirty-one sacks of salt stood against the wall, two of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: forty-six days at the ration, or a hundred and nine at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

options.label: Small in words, big digits
options.consequence: Words up to one hundred and for round numbers; digits for exact large figures and every system value (Level, EU, AU/s). Stages and tiers stay names (R47-7). Sourced numbers stand out as data.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to 412 rounds, split. Thirty-one sacks of salt stood against the wall, two of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: forty-six days at the ration, or 109 at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

options.label: Digits for every measure
options.consequence: Digits for every count, measure and system value; words only for rough numbers (a dozen, a few hundred). Crunchy and scannable, LitRPG-style; the prose starts to read like a report.
options.sample: The quartermaster walked the stack twice and wrote nothing until the second pass. The stack came to 412 rounds, split. 31 sacks of salt stood against the wall, 2 of them wet through. He did the sum on the board with his thumbnail: 46 days at the ration, or 109 at the ration they would all be on by the Thin Weeks.

questions.rec_reason: The prose stays literary, and wherever a sourced system figure appears it reads as hard data, the LitRPG pleasure without turning narration into a report.

questions.title: Capitals for system terms
questions.question: Which system terms take a capital letter in narration?
questions.context: The house capitalises most system words now: Stage, Band, Grade, Level, Wellspring, Essence, Pressure, and named Stages such as Murmuring. Check 37 validates listed terms such as Wellspring names (R18-7-CHECK37), and a near-miss fails (R14-5). LitRPG capitalises every system noun; literary fantasy capitalises proper names only.

options.label: Every system term
options.consequence: As now: Stage, Band, Grade, Level, Wellspring, Essence, Pressure, Sub-Stat names. System words read as terms; ordinary senses (a stage, a band of riders) stay lower case and need care.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's Pressure reached the desk. That put him in Murmuring. The coil on the counter gave his Band and his Grade before he had his gloves off, and his Level after that, slower, the needle settling by hairs. He had drawn from a Wellspring that morning; the Essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

options.label: Proper names only
options.consequence: Named Stages, named Wellsprings, Archons and Sub-Stat names capitalised; common system nouns lower case (stage, band, grade, level, wellspring, essence). A calmer literary page; the checker must tell term from word by context.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's pressure reached the desk. That put him in Murmuring. The coil on the counter gave his band and his grade before he had his gloves off, and his level after that, slower, the needle settling by hairs. He had drawn from a wellspring that morning; the essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

options.label: Caps follow the POV
options.consequence: A Guild or practitioner POV capitalises system terms; a commoner's narration lowers them, because to him they are plain words. Characterising, and uneven across a book by design. The sample is the gate-boy's POV.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man came in, and the gate-boy's ears rang with the weight the old men called a stage's push. The brass thing on the counter twitched and settled. The man had been at the well that morning; he smelled of it, flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain. The boy could not have told a band from a grade if either bit him.

options.label: Full LitRPG capitals
options.consequence: Every system-touched noun capitalised: Reserve, the Draw, Holding Coil, Traits, Paths, titles. Strongest game feel and easiest to scan; heavy on the eye, and a capital no longer marks a name.
options.sample: The clerk's pen stopped when the man's Pressure reached the desk. That put him in Murmuring. The Holding Coil gave his Band and his Grade before he had his gloves off, then his Level, then his Reserve, the needle settling by hairs. He had taken the Draw at a Wellspring that morning; the Essence on him smelled flat and metallic, a cut wire left in rain.

questions.rec_reason: It is the house habit already, gives the system a visible LitRPG surface without capitalising every noun, and keeps capitals the checker can validate.

questions.title: New words: what kind, how many
questions.question: When a scene needs a word for something new, which kind of coinage does it reach for, and how many may one scene carry?
questions.context: R51-14: 'No ceiling on WOTR terms per page'; a mid-scene coinage is logged and becomes canon only if Isaac reuses it (R50-28). WOTR coins three ways: English compounds (night-stone, draw-hum), native words (kiilut, tallut) and capitalised labels lettered on instruments. A portmanteau fuses two words into one.

options.label: All three, by owner
options.consequence: English compounds for common things, a culture's native word where that culture owns the thing, capitalised labels for system and instrument things; no cap, all logged (R50-28). The blend in one rule.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and left the main-quiet behind it. In the Moto lane they called it shizumari and put up their shutters. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. On the gauge-housing the needle lay against CUTOFF, and across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: English compounds, sparing
options.consequence: Old-English-style compounds and the odd portmanteau first (night-stone, main-quiet), two or three new words a scene at most, each placed so context carries it. Every coinage lands; less strangeness per page.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and the main-quiet came down on the street. Kettles stopped ticking. Dogs lifted their heads. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. On the gauge-housing the needle lay flat, and across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: Native words, freely
options.consequence: Each culture's own tongue first, as many words as the scene's cultures supply: Moto, Dawi and Kharven words for new things. Strongest culture and Eastern flavour; the heaviest reading load.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once. The Moto lane said shizumari and put up its shutters, and the Dawi cooper at the end of the row cut a tallut on his door-post for the hour. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. Across the river the rich side kept its lights.

options.label: Plain capitalised labels
options.consequence: New things get plain English names with a capital, LitRPG-style: Cutoff, Draw Rate, Main Silence. Instantly clear and game-flavoured; little poetry in the coinages.
options.sample: At the second bell the main went dead. The draw-hum quit in every wall at once and the street went into Cutoff, the Board's word, painted on every gauge-housing in the quarter. Kettles stopped ticking. A lampwright on the corner swore and went for his tallow. Across the river the rich side kept its lights, its Draw Rate a copper dearer on the thousand.

questions.rec_reason: Each tradition coins its own way, compounds for the West, native words for the East and labels for the game layer, and giving each its own territory blends them without a muddle.

questions.title: A word bank per culture
questions.question: Does each culture get a written word bank, the way it already has a senses bank?
questions.context: Each Standing Inventory carries senses, objects, oaths and proverbs, and scenes 'draw from it first' (R51-31). Native words sit scattered: Kharven kiilut and hulluk among the swears, Dawi tallut (the entry) and kaas (cask) among the objects. A word bank lists a culture's own words, trade terms and slang, with meaning and speaker.

options.label: A Words entry everywhere
options.consequence: Every Inventory gains a Words entry: native words, trade terms, slang and address forms, each with meaning and who says it. Scenes draw from it first; the checker can spell-check against it.
options.sample: Dawi, Words. tallut: the entry, a line cut in the Tally; any Dawi. kaas: the cask; brewers, anyone at table. thrus: a cut rune; burin-hands. ikke: one turn of a process; smiths and brewers. In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart, and told the Accord quartermaster the brew wanted one more ikke.

options.label: Only cultures with tongues
options.consequence: Banks for cultures that keep their own language (Kharven, Dawi, Moto, Elven, the Korean and Chinese strata); English-speaking cultures keep trade slang under Objects. Less to build; Accord slang stays unlisted.
options.sample: Dawi, Words: tallut, kaas, thrus, ikke, each with meaning and speaker, as for every culture that keeps its own tongue. Accord: no Words entry; its trade slang stays under Objects (the chit, a copper on the thousand). In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart. The quartermaster signed his chit.

options.label: One shared lexicon
options.consequence: One WOTR lexicon file, every culture's words in one list tagged by culture and linked from each Inventory. One place to check spelling and collisions (R51-11); scenes filter it by culture.
options.sample: WOTR Lexicon, one file. hulluk (Kharven): wet wood, the older word. kaas (Dawi): the cask. kiilut (Kharven): one of the dead left without the Waiting. tallut (Dawi): the entry. Each Inventory links to its own rows. In a scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart.

options.label: No bank, by ear
options.consequence: Words borrowed or coined in the scene and logged (R50-28), with no standing list. Freest drafting; spellings drift, and the checker has nothing to hold.
options.sample: No standing list. Scene log, the Seat cellars: tallut and kaas, already in the Dawi Inventory; keg-quiet, coined this scene, canon if Isaac reuses it. In the scene: The tallyman cut the tallut before the kaas was off the cart, and the cellar went keg-quiet while he counted.

questions.rec_reason: A bank per culture keeps Eastern and Northern words consistent from scene to scene and gives the checker a list to hold, the way the senses bank already works.

questions.title: Swear words in close-POV narration
questions.question: Which stocks of swear words may close-POV narration use?
questions.context: Profanity may bleed into close-POV narration, 'timeless profanities plus swears invented deliberately for WOTR' (R51-02); each culture's own oaths come first (R51-29); Earth holy swears are out (R51-30); drafted culture sets await approval (R51-35). Real Japanese, Korean and Chinese swears have no ruling: kuso (shit), ssibal (fuck), tamade (damn it).

options.label: English hard words
options.consequence: English profanity in the POV's head, as R51-02 already allows: shit, fuck, piss. Universal and blunt; used alone, it makes every culture curse alike.
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Shit. He lay there a breath with the cold coming up through his coat, then got a thumb to the seal. Whole. Fuck, but it was whole, and the ribs would tell him about it by morning.

options.label: The culture's own swears
options.consequence: Each culture's oaths and insults lead (R51-29): Kharven canon now, the other cultures' drafted sets once approved (R51-35). The Moto words in this sample come from that draft.
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Incorrect, his father would have said, one word and no heat. Frozen piss, the riders called this yard, and he had thought them coarse for it. He got a thumb to the seal. Whole. By the Fourteen, whole.

options.label: Real East Asian swears
options.consequence: Eastern-register POVs may curse in Japanese, Korean or Chinese, romanised and never italic. Real heat and real sound; each word must be correct and fit the period (R50-01).
options.sample: His heel went on the yard ice and the rest of him followed. He landed on the dispatch case, ribs first. Kuso. He lay there a breath with the cold coming up through his coat, then got a thumb to the seal. Whole. Kuso, kuso, but whole, and the ribs would tell him about it by morning.

questions.rec_reason: Together they let an Eastern POV reach for a real Japanese or Korean curse, a WOTR one or an English one, which is the blend in a single word, with the culture's own still first.

questions.title: Stock-phrase families for the ban list
questions.question: Which families of stock phrases join the hard-ban list?
questions.context: R51-10's hard-ban list (fifteen stock words and phrases) FAILs at first use in narration and speech. A blend imports new filler from each tradition. Pick none to keep the list as it stands, or type an item to trim. The samples show a flagged line and the same beat written clean.

options.label: Cultivation-translation stock
options.consequence: Bans 'a cold glint flashed', 'sucked in a cold breath', 'courting death', 'killing intent surged', 'an ant before an elephant'. The Eastern feel comes from method, never from translated filler.
options.sample: Flagged: The elder sucked in a cold breath, and a cold glint flashed in his eyes. Clean: The elder set his cup down without looking at it. Tea ran over the lip and along the table, and he let it run. His eyes stayed on the boy's feet, where the floorboards had split along the grain.

options.label: Western fantasy stock
options.consequence: Bans 'the steel sang', 'a grim smile', 'blood ran cold', 'every fibre of his being', 'darkness gathered'. Grimdark's own worn phrasing goes out with the imported kind.
options.sample: Flagged: A grim smile touched the elder's lips, and his blood ran cold. Clean: The elder set his cup down without looking at it. Tea ran over the lip and along the table, and he let it run. His eyes stayed on the boy's feet, where the floorboards had split along the grain.

options.label: LitRPG stock
options.consequence: Bans 'power surged through him', 'a notification chimed', 'stronger than ever', 'the numbers went up'. Progress shows in the body and on the instrument.
options.sample: Flagged: Power surged through the boy, and he was stronger than ever. Clean: The boy's hands had stopped shaking. Under him the floorboards had split along the grain, and across the hall the elder set his cup down without looking at it and let the tea run.

questions.rec_reason: A blend imports each tradition's filler along with its strengths; banning all three families keeps the borrowing at the level of method.

questions.title: What the checker enforces
questions.question: Which vocabulary checks does verify_scene gain?
questions.context: verify_scene (build/verify.py, the house prose checker) FAILs the hard-ban list, WARNs on modern words in narration, Earth calendar words and holy swears, and under --combat WARNs on zero HEMA words. Loanword spelling, italics, capitals and number style go unchecked. A FAIL blocks a Natalie reply; a WARN asks for a read.

options.label: Word-bank spelling check
options.consequence: Native words and loanwords are matched against the culture banks (VB11); a near-miss FAILs like a misspelt Wellspring (R14-5); unknown words are listed for the scene log (R50-28).
options.sample:
FAIL near-miss: "kilut" in "...he would have been kilut, and every woman..." (bank has kiilut, Kharven; R14-5-NEAR_MISS_FAIL)
info words in no bank: main-quiet, shizumari (log with the scene, R50-28)

options.label: Eastern fight lists
options.consequence: The --combat check counts kenjutsu, Korean and Chinese martial terms beside HEMA, so a duel written in its own school's words (VB6) stops warning.
options.sample:
info combat density: 0 HEMA terms, 6 kenjutsu terms (jōdan, ma-ai, kiri-oroshi, tsuba, sen no sen, chiburi), 5 anatomy terms
no WARN: the duel names its moves in its own school's words (R48-33-CHOREOGRAPHY)

options.label: New ban families FAIL
options.consequence: The families chosen in VB13 FAIL at first use, as R51-10 does; looser variants of a banned phrase WARN for a read.
options.sample:
FAIL hard-ban phrase: "a cold glint flashed" in "...breath, and a cold glint flashed in his eyes..." (R51-10-SLOP_WORDS, cultivation family)
WARN stock watch: "grim smile" (Western family; keep only if it is the POV's own idiom)

options.label: Style-sheet warnings
options.consequence: WARNs for the house style set here: an italicised loanword, a lower-case system term, a digit where words are due. Holds VB3, VB8 and VB9 without blocking a reply.
options.sample:
WARN italic loanword: "*kiilut*" (R49-49-FOREIGN)
WARN lower-case system term: "his band" (house capitals, VB9)
WARN number style: "31 sacks" (words up to one hundred, VB8)

questions.rec_reason: Each check holds one of this section's choices in place mechanically, so the blend's vocabulary survives long sessions instead of drifting back to defaults.

settled.point: Earth day and month names never appear, and 'week' becomes the culture's own span.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled 2026-09-26 and already warned by the checker; the blend changes nothing about the calendar.

settled.point: Earth holy swears are replaced by the world's own powers.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; VB12 asks only which stocks of swear words narration may draw on.

settled.point: The short slang and pop-psych lists stay out of narration, and narration stays timeless.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled and checked; VB5 asks how antique narration runs, and VB13 adds stock-phrase families instead of reopening these lists.

settled.point: Collision words keep only their WOTR sense.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; no blend choice touches it.

settled.point: Borrowed words are real, correct and romanised, with no kanji or hangul on the page and diacritics kept.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; every loanword option in this section inherits these conditions.

settled.point: Stat, Sub-Stat and Guild words and sourced figures are free in narration, and no number is invented.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; whether they appear on screens is the LitRPG section's question, and VB8 asks only how numbers are written in prose.

settled.point: Technique names and their translations are free in narration, and mechanism terms may stand bare mid-action.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; how techniques are named belongs to the names sections.

settled.point: Real science, anatomy and trade words are legal in narration on its own authority, and a trained POV names his own wound exactly.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled and floored by Check 30; VB7 covers units and VB6 the martial lexicon, the parts the blend reopens.

settled.point: A chant appears in its own language, each practitioner's own.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; VB4 asks only about learned tags in narration.

settled.point: Old English or Latinate word stock is by ear, the elevated word bank is by ear, and Earth-derived words are legal.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled by ear; the blend puts no pressure on them.

settled.point: Technology and office metaphors appear only where the POV's culture has the thing.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; it already scales to any culture the blend adds.

settled.point: In-world documents keep a house style per institution and take the modern-word list.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; documents are their own section's matter.

settled.point: Ozone and other technical smell words are free; only the stock ozone phrase stays banned.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled in C-090; VB13 extends the ban list without touching it.

settled.point: Explicit narration stays plain and crude, in working-man anatomical words.
settled.why_not_asked: Ruled; no blend choice changes it.
